notes:
Task and constraints: Score a baseball game from integer rounds and the operations C, D, and +.
Idea: Keep a list of valid round scores and apply each operation to the latest entries.
Technique and why it applies: C removes the last score, D appends twice the last score, and + appends the sum of the last two scores. Numeric strings are parsed and appended directly.
Invariant: temp contains the round scores that remain valid after processing the current operation.
Edge cases: The input guarantees operations have enough prior scores for C, D, and +. remove(last_value) removes the first matching value, not necessarily the last occurrence, so duplicate scores can cause incorrect behavior; pop() is safer.
Complexity: Each operation is processed once, giving O(n) time and O(n) history space.

Task and constraints: Compute the total score for a sequence of baseball operations.
Idea: Maintain a score stack and apply each operation to its top entries.
Technique and why it applies: + combines the last two scores, D doubles the last score, and C pops the most recent score. Other tokens are parsed as integer scores.
Invariant: history stores all scores that have not been canceled.
Edge cases: The operation sequence is assumed valid, so required prior scores exist when C, D, or + appears. pop() correctly removes the latest score.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the history stack.

Task and constraints: Find the edge that creates a cycle in an undirected graph that was originally a tree.
Idea: Use disjoint-set union to track connected components while processing edges in order.
Technique and why it applies: If both endpoints already have the same representative, the new edge closes a cycle and is returned. Otherwise union merges their components, using path compression and rank.
Invariant: The disjoint-set structure represents connectivity induced by all previously processed edges.
Edge cases: Vertex labels are shifted down by one to index the arrays. The implementation sizes arrays by distinct vertex count, assuming labels form 1..n as guaranteed by the problem.
Complexity: With path compression and rank, the operations are near O(1) amortized, so total time is O(n α(n)) and space O(n).

Task and constraints: Remove one directed edge so the graph becomes a rooted tree, handling a possible node with two parents or a directed cycle.
Idea: Count incoming edges, test candidate edges when a node has indegree two, otherwise use DSU to detect a cycle.
Technique and why it applies: The code removes a candidate edge conceptually and checks whether its endpoints remain connected, then chooses one of the two incoming edges. In the no-two-parent case, DSU detects an edge whose endpoints are already connected.
Invariant: count records each node's indegree; DSU tracks undirected connectivity of processed edges.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without a global import, so this snippet can raise NameError. The connectedness test and candidate choice appear reversed for the standard two-parent case, so correctness is questionable; the no-cycle path also has no explicit final return.
Complexity: DSU processing is near O(n α(n)) time and O(n) space, but missing imports and selection logic affect correctness.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of repetitions of A needed so B appears as a substring, or return -1.
Idea: Handle the case where A is at least as long as B, then estimate the needed repetitions from B's length and alignment.
Technique and why it applies: If B is already inside A or A+A, one or two copies suffice. Otherwise the code estimates prefix and suffix overhang around occurrences of A and verifies the candidate by direct substring search.
Invariant: repeat is the proposed number of A copies sufficient to cover B's length and possible alignment offset.
Edge cases: Empty strings are outside the usual constraints. The direct membership check guards against a mistaken estimate, returning -1 if the candidate repetitions do not contain B.
Complexity: String search over repeated strings can take O(|A|·repeat + |B|) time and space proportional to the constructed repetition.

Task and constraints: Find the probability that a knight remains on an n-by-n board after exactly k moves.
Idea: Memoize the survival probability for each cell and move count.
Technique and why it applies: Each of the eight possible knight moves is equally likely. Out-of-board moves contribute zero, and at move count k a valid cell contributes one; recursive averages yield the survival probability.
Invariant: cache[(i,j,moves)] stores the probability of staying on the board through the remaining moves from that state as defined by the recursion.
Edge cases: k=0 returns 1 for a valid starting cell. The start position is assumed inside the board.
Complexity: There are O(n²k) states and eight transitions per state, giving O(n²k) time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the probability a knight stays on an N-by-N chessboard after K moves.
Idea: Use two rolling DP layers, starting with probability one at every cell for zero remaining moves.
Technique and why it applies: For each step and cell, sum one eighth of the previous-layer probabilities at all legal knight destinations. Alternating layers avoids retaining every time step.
Invariant: dp[step%2][i][j] is the probability of staying on the board for the current number of moves when starting at cell (i,j).
Edge cases: K=0 returns one. Moves landing outside the board are omitted, so their probability mass is lost.
Complexity: Each step visits N² cells and eight directions, giving O(KN²) time and O(N²) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Select three non-overlapping length-k subarrays with maximum total sum and return their starting indices.
Idea: Compute each window sum with prefix sums, then memoize a recursion choosing a window or skipping its start.
Technique and why it applies: Taking a window advances by k to prevent overlap; skipping advances by one. On equal totals the code takes the current window, favoring earlier indices.
Invariant: dfs(i,t) returns the best sum and corresponding indices using t windows starting no earlier than i.
Edge cases: The constraints guarantee three valid windows. If no valid solution existed, negative infinity would propagate, but the input size is expected to permit a selection.
Complexity: There are O(n) positions times four remaining-count states, with constant work per state, so O(n) time and O(n) memo space, excluding stored index lists.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of stickers needed to spell target, using letters from each sticker as available counts.
Idea: Memoize recursion on the remaining target string and try stickers containing its first character.
Technique and why it applies: For each candidate sticker, subtract its letter frequencies from the target's counts and recursively solve the sorted remaining letters. Restricting to stickers with the first target character avoids equivalent branches that make no progress on that character.
Invariant: dfs(target) is the minimum stickers required to form the exact remaining target string.
Edge cases: Empty target returns zero. The code calls dfs(s) in the conditional and again in the chosen expression, but memoization makes the repeated call reuse its cached result.
Complexity: The state space is exponential in target length in the worst case; each state tries all stickers and processes a fixed alphabet, with memo space proportional to distinct residual strings.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, ordered by descending frequency and then lexicographically.
Idea: Count each word, build a min-heap of negative frequencies and words, then pop k entries.
Technique and why it applies: Heap tuples compare negative counts first, putting higher frequencies first; ties are broken lexicographically by word. Repeated occurrences update the dictionary count.
Invariant: li maps each distinct word to its frequency, and heap contains one ranking tuple per distinct word.
Edge cases: k is assumed not to exceed the number of distinct words. Tuple ordering implements the required alphabetical tie-break.
Complexity: Counting takes O(n), heap construction O(u), and k pops O(k log u), with O(u) space for u distinct words.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, using a bounded heap.
Idea: Count words and keep a heap of at most k candidates, ordered so the least desirable selected word is removed first.
Technique and why it applies: MinHeapObj reverses lexical ordering for equal frequencies so the heap root is the worst among selected words; adding a k+1th candidate removes that root. Reversing the final pop order produces the desired ranking.
Invariant: The heap retains the best k words processed so far under frequency-descending and word-ascending order.
Edge cases: The code imports several unused names. If k is valid, the heap never needs more than k entries after each insertion.
Complexity: Counting is O(n); heap maintenance is O(u log k), and output extraction costs O(k log k). Space is O(u) for counts and O(k) for the heap.

Task and constraints: Find the k most frequent words with ties resolved lexicographically.
Idea: Bucket words by frequency, collect high-frequency buckets until at least k candidates exist, then sort candidates by ranking.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency buckets avoid a heap. Each candidate is stored as (-frequency, word), so ordinary tuple sorting gives descending frequency and ascending lexical order.
Invariant: pairs contains all words from the highest frequency buckets visited so far.
Edge cases: The loop ranges from len(words)-1 down to zero, excluding the bucket at frequency len(words). If every input word is identical, its bucket is skipped and the method can return an empty list incorrectly.
Complexity: Bucket construction is O(n), collecting and sorting candidates is O(u log u) in the worst case, with O(n+u) space.

Task and constraints: Return the k most frequent words, using quickselect to isolate the top-ranked entries.
Idea: Count words, create tuples (-frequency, word), partition them around the kth tuple, and sort the first k entries.
Technique and why it applies: Tuple ordering ranks higher frequency first and lexical order for ties. Randomized partitioning places the kth element at its final rank on average, after which sorting the prefix gives ordered output.
Invariant: After kthElement returns, the first k tuples contain the k smallest ranking tuples.
Edge cases: k is assumed between one and the number of distinct words. Random pivot selection affects performance but not intended ordering.
Complexity: Quickselect is O(u) average and O(u²) worst case for u distinct words; sorting the selected k costs O(k log k), and storage is O(u).

Task and constraints: Check whether the binary representation of n alternates between zero and one at every adjacent bit.
Idea: Convert n to a binary string and reject any adjacent equal characters.
Technique and why it applies: Alternating bits means every neighboring pair differs, so the scan returns False when it sees 00 or 11 and True if no such pair exists.
Invariant: Every pair of bits before the current index has already been confirmed to alternate.
Edge cases: A one-bit number returns True because there are no adjacent pairs. n is positive under the usual constraints.
Complexity: Binary conversion and scanning take O(log n) time and O(log n) space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether n's binary digits alternate.
Idea: Repeatedly divide n by two and compare each current least-significant bit with the next bit.
Technique and why it applies: divmod returns the quotient and current bit. If two consecutive extracted bits match, the representation is not alternating; otherwise the scan continues until the quotient is zero.
Invariant: curr is the most recently extracted bit, and n holds the unprocessed higher-order bits.
Edge cases: A one-bit value returns True. The method assumes n is nonnegative; n=0 also returns True.
Complexity: One iteration per bit gives O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the largest connected component of land cells in a binary grid.
Idea: Start DFS at each unvisited land cell, mark cells as visited, and count the connected area.
Technique and why it applies: Each land cell is changed to '#', preventing it from being counted again. The recursive calls explore four orthogonal neighbors and sum their areas.
Invariant: dfs returns the size of the land component reachable from its starting cell, while visited cells are no longer equal to 1.
Edge cases: Empty grid returns zero. The code assumes rectangular rows and may hit recursion-depth limits on a very large island.
Complexity: Each cell is visited a constant number of times, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case recursion space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum area of a connected island in a binary grid.
Idea: DFS from each positive cell, mark visited land by negating its value, and count cells in that component.
Technique and why it applies: The recursive helper rejects out-of-bounds, water, and already-visited cells. Each valid cell is negated and contributes one to the shared area counter before exploring four neighbors.
Invariant: Negative cells are visited land; area[0] counts cells discovered in the current component.
Edge cases: The grid is assumed nonempty because the code accesses grid[0]. Mutating values prevents later scans from recounting the same island.
Complexity: Every cell is explored at most once, giving O(RC) time and O(RC) worst-case recursion space.

Task and constraints: Count substrings containing equal numbers of consecutive zeros and ones, where each run consists of one bit value.
Idea: Track lengths of the previous and current runs and add the smaller run length whenever the bit changes.
Technique and why it applies: For adjacent runs of lengths a and b, exactly min(a,b) substrings cross their boundary with equal zeros and ones. The final update accounts for the last pair of runs.
Invariant: pre_cont_occ and cur_cont_occ are the lengths of adjacent bit runs, and counter totals contributions from completed run boundaries.
Edge cases: A one-character string returns zero. The code has tab indentation in a comment; if executable indentation is inconsistent, it may cause an indentation error.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count substrings with equal consecutive runs of zeros and ones.
Idea: Track previous-run length and current-run length, adding their minimum at every transition between bits.
Technique and why it applies: A substring with equal zeros and ones must span the boundary between two runs, and the shorter run limits how many such substrings can be formed there.
Invariant: prev is the prior run length and curr is the current run length; result sums contributions for every completed boundary.
Edge cases: A string with only one run returns zero because prev stays zero. The final min(prev,curr) handles the last run boundary.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose length equals the array's degree.
Idea: Group indices by value, find the highest frequency, then minimize the first-to-last span among values with that frequency.
Technique and why it applies: A value's degree is its occurrence count; the shortest subarray containing all occurrences spans from its first index to its last. The smallest span among maximum-frequency values is the answer.
Invariant: d[value] stores occurrence indices in ascending order, and best tracks the shortest span among degree-achieving values.
Edge cases: The code uses defaultdict without importing it, so it requires that name externally or raises NameError. nums is assumed nonempty because max is called on the dictionary values.
Complexity: Index collection and the final scan take O(n) time and O(n) space.
